primary.name: 1973 National Personnel Records Center fire — 16-18 million military personnel files
primary.known_fact: An estimated 16-18 million OMPFs of Army/Army Air Force/Air Force personnel discharged 1912-1964 damaged or destroyed; ~6.5 million survived in varying condition. 80% loss for Army 1912-1960; 75% for Air Force 1947-1964. NPRC reconstructs service from alternate sources (~5.5 million reconstructions).
primary.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the destroyed files held service details not present in the alternate sources used for reconstruction; the reconstruction records themselves show the primary channel cannot be enumerated. Source establishes destruction scale and the reconstruction practice, not any specific destroyed file's contents.
primary.discard_mechanism: fire at 9700 Page Avenue, St. Louis, July 12 1973; burned 22+ hours out of control; water + mold damaged survivors; source never determined
primary.notes: Primary source (NARA). 'Unparalleled disaster' per Archivist David S. Ferriero. Reconstruction from alternate sources proves G8: more records elsewhere cannot reconstruct the destroyed channel itself.

ranked.name: 2008 Universal backlot fire destroyed ~175,000 master recording tapes
ranked.known_fact: NYT Magazine investigation (June 2019, Jody Rosen): more than 175,000 master tapes destroyed, estimated ~500,000 song titles. Almost all Buddy Holly masters; most of John Coltrane's Impulse catalog; all Decca masters (Holiday, Armstrong, Ellington, Fitzgerald, Berry); multitracks; sessions never released. UMG had told Billboard in 2008 it 'had no loss.'
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: unreleased sessions and isolated-instrument multitracks that were never cataloged publicly are gone and can never be enumerated from the surviving commercial catalog. NOT claimed: specific unreleased tracks exist — only that the vault inventory, per the NYT investigation, included never-released sessions whose contents no surviving record enumerates.
ranked.discard_mechanism: accidental fire, June 1 2008; archive had been downplayed as a 'video vault' of copies
ranked.notes: Cited source is Metal Insider's account of the NYT Magazine investigation (paywalled at NYT). Corroborated by the class-action complaint filing against UMG (digitalmusicnews PDF, 2019). Commercial releases survive; the master-quality channel and unreleased-session remainder do not.

ranked.name: Apollo 11 raw slow-scan telemetry tapes degaussed and reused
ranked.known_fact: A 2009 NASA search concluded ~45 raw slow-scan telemetry tapes were likely degaussed and reused circa 1981-82 to support Landsat and the shuttle program. The live-converted NTSC broadcast survives in many archives; the raw higher-quality SSTV channel does not. NASA emphasized no unseen moonwalk video was lost.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the raw SSTV signal held higher-resolution signal information than the converted broadcast; that higher-quality information is unrecoverable. NOT claimed: unseen scenes or suppressed footage — NASA says no unseen moonwalk video was lost, and the record is treated as authoritative on that point.
ranked.discard_mechanism: degaussed and recertified for reuse by NASA/Goddard in early 1980s tape scarcity
ranked.notes: Primary DCC instance. Procedural erasure of a channel that existed, not undersampling. The lost remainder is signal quality / future reprocessing capacity, not unknown scenes.

ranked.name: 1890 US Census schedules destroyed in 1921 Commerce Department fire
ranked.known_fact: Only 6,160 persons listed in surviving population-census fragments (M407, 3 rolls, fragments in 10 states + DC). Veterans schedules, Oklahoma territorial schedules, and Delaware African-American lists partially survived. A 20-year genealogical gap 1880-1900 resulted.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the destroyed schedules held the only enumerations of millions of 1890 households; no other record enumerates what was on the destroyed pages. Source establishes the destruction, not any specific destroyed person's data.
ranked.discard_mechanism: fire in Commerce Department basement, January 10 1921 (25% burned, 50% water-damaged); Congress authorized disposal 1933; destroyed 1934-35
ranked.notes: Primary institutional source (NARA). Note the two-stage discard: 1921 fire damage, then deliberate disposal authorized by Congress in 1933.

ranked.name: 70% of American silent feature films lost (Library of Congress 2013)
ranked.known_fact: LoC's first comprehensive survey of 10,919 American silent features: ~70% believed lost; only 14% (1,575 titles) survive in original 35mm; 11% survive only as foreign versions or lower-quality formats. 'An alarming and irretrievable loss to our nation's cultural record' (Librarian of Congress James H. Billington).
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the lost 70% contained creative works no surviving catalog enumerates; each lost title is an unenumerated remainder. Source establishes the scale of loss, not any specific film's contents.
ranked.discard_mechanism: decay, studio fires, deliberate destruction/melting for silver content, neglect
ranked.notes: Aggregate-instance: DCC claims the class-level shape, not any single title. The LoC study is the primary institutional source.

ranked.name: Pioneer 10/11 and Helios instrumentation reels abandoned, later found mold-damaged in engineer's basement
ranked.known_fact: NASA OIG report: 325 reels picked up Dec 8, 2015; most unmarked; majority appear to be Pioneer 10/11 instrumentation reels; 'poor condition and almost all affected by moderate to severe mould.' The engineer was told he could have them when IBM was getting rid of the items.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: most reels are unmarked, so their contents cannot be enumerated from any surviving inventory; whether the mold-damaged telemetry remains readable is unknown. NOT claimed: that the data is already lost — recovery status is unknown.
ranked.discard_mechanism: IBM/NASA disposed of the reels circa 1968-1972; an IBM engineer took ~325 reels home; found mold-damaged in a Pittsburgh basement, recovered by NASA OIG December 2015
ranked.notes: Primary source (NASA OIG FOIA report). Lowest-certainty instance: the channel physically survives in degraded form, so DCC holds only for the unenumerated, possibly-unreadable remainder.

ranked.name: DuMont Television Network archive destroyed — ~20,000 episodes to ~350 survivors
ranked.known_fact: Of 20,000+ episodes, ~350 survive, mostly in personal collections (Jackie Gleason preserved his own Honeymooners sketches). Edie Adams testified to the Library of Congress in 1996 about the alleged 1970s dumping; the bay-dumping account is commonly reported lore — the source notes 'no one really knows for sure what happened.'
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the destroyed archive contained early-television programming whose contents no surviving record enumerates; early programs (Captain Video, Cavalcade of Stars) survive only in fragments. The dumping mechanism is partly unverified lore and is NOT presented as settled fact.
ranked.discard_mechanism: much destroyed ~1958 to recover silver content; remaining kinescopes reportedly dumped into Upper New York Bay in the 1970s after custody passed to successor companies
ranked.notes: Internet Archive blog is credible-secondary; it explicitly flags the bay-dumping as unverified lore. The silver-recovery destruction ~1958 is the firmer mechanism.

ranked.name: 1937 Fox vault fire, Little Ferry NJ — most Fox silent films pre-1932 destroyed
ranked.known_fact: All archived film in the vaults destroyed; loss of most silent films produced by Fox Film Corporation before 1932, plus negatives from Educational Pictures and other studios. 1 death, 2 injuries.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the destroyed vault contents included titles whose only records were the destroyed elements; the full contents of the vault were never enumerated before the fire.
ranked.discard_mechanism: spontaneous combustion of decaying nitrate in heat wave, July 9 1937; no sprinklers or ventilation
ranked.notes: Wikipedia is secondary; the event is corroborated across film-preservation literature. Theda Bara's near-total filmography loss is commonly cited from this fire.

ranked.name: 1965 MGM Vault 7 fire, Culver City — only known copies of hundreds of films destroyed
ranked.known_fact: The only known copies of hundreds of silent and early-sound films were destroyed, including London After Midnight (1927), The Divine Woman (1928), the last known print of The Rogue Song, and original-release prints of pre-1951 MGM cartoons including the silent Our Gang shorts 1927-1929.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: 'only known copies' per the source means no surviving record can enumerate the destroyed reels' full contents; specific destroyed-only titles are known from secondary records, but their complete vault contents were not enumerated before the fire.
ranked.discard_mechanism: electrical short ignited stored nitrate, August 10 1965; entire vault contents destroyed
ranked.notes: Secondary source (Wikipedia); event corroborated in lost-film literature (e.g., collider.com lost-films history).

ranked.name: NBC wiped Johnny Carson Tonight Show master tapes, 1962-1972
ranked.known_fact: Only 33 episodes originally aired prior to May 1, 1972 are known to survive erasure by NBC, including Carson's debut (audio survives). The archive is virtually complete 1973-1992 after Carson took control of masters.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the erased decade contained interviews and performances not documented in surviving records; the erased contents cannot be enumerated because the masters were the record. NOT claimed: any specific lost moment — the Dean Martin April 1973 anecdote is unverified YouTube lore and is NOT used as evidence.
ranked.discard_mechanism: routine tape reuse/erasure per standard industry procedure; Carson discovered in 1972 that NBC held no archive
ranked.notes: Some kinescopes survive via Armed Forces Radio and Television Service and guest collections (DVIDS, 1963 reel recovery). Secondary source; the DVIDS military-recovery story corroborates the erasure.

ranked.name: BBC wiped Doctor Who episodes 1967-1978
ranked.known_fact: Search result reported 95 of 253 early episodes missing; other tallies use 97 or 106 depending on date and counting method. Audio recordings, stills, and telesnaps survive for many episodes; some recovered from overseas broadcasters and private collections.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: the missing broadcast-quality masters are the unenumerated remainder — surviving audio/stills enumerate content, not the visual channel as transmitted. Discrepant counts (95/97/106) are preserved, not resolved.
ranked.discard_mechanism: systematic junking policy: tape reuse, storage space, materials scarcity, rights constraints
ranked.notes: Partial survival (audio, stills, some recovered episodes) weakens G5; the DCC claim is specifically the broadcast-master channel, not the episodes as known works.

ranked.name: MySpace server migration made 2003-2015 user uploads unavailable
reasons: Soft archive overlap: PLATFORM — Platform dual: content partly known to uploaders, partial duplicates; penalized
ranked.known_fact: Reports estimate 50+ million songs from ~14 million artists (uploads 2003-2015) became unavailable. MySpace's documented explanation is a server migration. Intentional-deletion speculation is NOT repeated here — it is unsupported.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: demos and early works with no independent copies are no longer publicly recoverable; but whether every item lacked an independent copy is unknown — many uploaders retained originals.
ranked.discard_mechanism: server migration; MySpace stated older photos, videos, and audio became unavailable
ranked.notes: Soft penalty PLATFORM: much content was known to uploaders and many originals survive privately; the lost remainder is the public-corpus channel.

ranked.name: NLM retired TOXNET December 16, 2019; Toxmap interface discontinued
reasons: Recovery materially possible or partial duplicate exists
More data elsewhere reconstructs the discarded channel
Soft archive overlap: MIGRATION — Migration dual: substantial content re-homed; residual is the interface loss; penalized
ranked.known_fact: NLM Technical Bulletin: TOXNET retired Dec 16, 2019. Most content migrated to PubChem, PubMed, Bookshelf, or returned to source organizations (e.g., EPA). 'Some databases will be retired.' Toxmap — the pollution-mapping interface researchers relied on for visualization — was shuttered without a migration path (Popular Science, 2019).
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: retired databases and the Toxmap interface's query/visualization functionality constituted a channel (API access patterns, curated interface state) not fully enumerated by the migrated content.
ranked.discard_mechanism: planned retirement; most databases migrated to PubChem/PubMed/Bookshelf; TOXNET API, mobile site, and LactMed apps retired; some databases retired outright
ranked.notes: Soft penalty MIGRATION: most content demonstrably re-homed (fails G8 partially — elsewhere reconstructs much). The DCC remainder is the retired databases plus the Toxmap interface channel.

ranked.name: GeoCities shut down October 2009; ~38 million pages deleted
reasons: Soft archive overlap: PLATFORM — Platform dual: content partly known to uploaders, partial duplicates; penalized
ranked.known_fact: The Internet Archive attempted to save as many of ~38 million pages as possible; the independent Archive Team rescued about a terabyte in a six-month crawl. Yahoo refused to release directory lists; crawls were incomplete and different rescue projects captured different fractions.
ranked.inference_statement: INFERENCE: uncrawled pages — those never visited by any rescue crawler — are gone without enumeration, since Yahoo released no directory. The crawled fraction is not the channel.
ranked.discard_mechanism: Yahoo shut down GeoCities US on October 26, 2009; data not personally archived by owners declared irrecoverable
ranked.notes: Soft penalty PLATFORM: volunteer rescue captured a substantial-but-incomplete fraction; the uncrawled remainder is the DCC remainder.

iterate_known_content.case: A fully-cataloged library burns; every volume's full text survives in an off-site digital archive.
iterate_known_content.why: Retained catalog fully enumerates the channel. Ordinary loss.

iterate_known_content.case: An uncataloged vault of field recordings burns; no inventory existed.
iterate_known_content.why: No surviving record enumerates what was lost. The unknown content is inference.

iterate_known_content.case: A tape set is wiped, but a complete bit-identical clone survives.
iterate_known_content.why: Fails G5 (irrecoverability), not G4. Controls exist in the instance set.

iterate_discard_intent_ablation.finding: Both intentional (wiping, dumping, migration) and accidental (fire, decay) discards sit in the eligible set with comparable scores. The class groups the LOSS SHAPE, not the motive — a limitation for policy use (intent matters for prevention) but the point of the discriminator: what is uninterrogable is uninterrogable regardless of why the channel died.

claim_hygiene: Research-stage classification. Not a physical discovery, not peer review, not a patent. Scores are a classification heuristic, not measurements of nature. Every unknown-content conclusion is labeled INFERENCE unless the source directly establishes it. No filing, publication, or repository change has occurred.
